runs.response:
You want me to pay fifty rand every month just to use an app that says it’ll pay me back for studying. Fifty rand doesn’t sound like much to the person asking, but in my house it’s a taxi fare. It’s data. It’s what Gogo needs to stretch when the grant and pension come in. We’re already pulling ten thousand rand a month through school fees that take four to eight thousand a year, and what’s left barely covers the forty-five-minute commute each way, let alone the airtime I need just to keep my phone connected. You’re asking for a recurring charge on a grant-dependent budget for a promise of financial rewards later. Promises don’t buy data bundles, and they don’t create a quiet room for me to focus when I finally get home.

I don’t study for a payout. I study because the alternative is nothing. Putting a price tag on motivation doesn’t make it real, and taking fifty rand out of a household that’s already counting every rand to keep me in this classroom isn’t something I can justify. If this platform was cheaper than the extra classes I’m already missing, or if it didn’t ask for a subscription before proving it actually works without eating my data, I might consider it. But right now, it’s just another thing asking me to spend what we don’t have on a system that already leaves us behind.

runs.response:
Fifty rand a month sounds small on paper, but on a ten thousand rand household income it still competes directly with groceries, transport, and school fees that already sit between five hundred and a thousand rand per child. I track every deadline, every load-shedding schedule, and every rand outflow closely, so I don’t just slot another recurring charge into our budget without knowing exactly what it delivers. What gives me pause isn’t just the amount, but the core idea of turning study effort into financial rewards. I want my children to open their books because they know education is the practical route forward, not because they’re waiting for a payout. When you attach money to homework or quizzes, you shift the focus from building discipline to chasing a transaction. External rewards might get them to click through a lesson today, but they don’t teach the kind of self-reliance they’ll need when there’s no one handing out incentives. I’ve seen enough in my own work processing permits and compliance files to know that sustainable progress comes from consistent habits, not short-term payoffs. I’m not dismissing the need for tools that make learning more accessible, and I firmly believe things are improving and there’s a real chance for our children to get ahead if they put in the hours. But I need to know whether this platform actually strengthens their study routines and works reliably on our shared device, or if it’s mostly a system that measures engagement and hands out cash. If it proves it builds real academic discipline without creating dependency on a payout, I’d look at it again when the school term settles and we can see where the household budget has breathing room. Wanting something that supports their progress and finding the space for it in our monthly outgoings are two different calculations, and I won’t rush either one.
